title: Nietzsche I: The Death of God and the Genealogy of Morals
subtitle: Where do our values come from, and what happens when their foundation gives way?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what Nietzsche meant by 'God is dead' and why he thought it was a crisis rather than a triumph
Describe the method of genealogy and how it differs from asking whether a value is justified
Explain the contrast between master morality ('good and bad') and slave morality ('good and evil') and the role of ressentiment
Explain perspectivism and distinguish it from simple 'anything goes' relativism
Assess the strongest objections to Nietzsche's account of morality
hook:
Imagine a madman running into a busy marketplace on a bright morning, carrying a lit lantern and crying, "I seek God! I seek God!" The people standing around, most of them not believers, laugh at him. Has God got lost? Has he gone on a voyage? Emigrated? The madman jumps into their midst and pierces them with his eyes. "Where is God?" he cries. "I will tell you. We have killed him, you and I. All of us are his murderers." When nobody understands, he throws his lantern to the ground. "I have come too early," he says. "My time is not yet."

This scene, from section 125 of Friedrich Nietzsche's *The Gay Science* (1882), contains the most famous three words in modern philosophy: God is dead. Notice who the madman is talking to. Not pious believers, but comfortable unbelievers who think nothing much has changed. Nietzsche's point is that they have not yet understood what they have done. Yesterday Kierkegaard (Day 64) tried to rescue genuine faith from a lukewarm Christendom. Today we meet the thinker who looked at the same lukewarm Christendom and concluded that the whole building was about to collapse.

sections.heading: The Philologist Who Philosophized with a Hammer
sections.body:
Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was born in 1844 in Röcken, a village in Prussian Saxony, the son of a Lutheran pastor. His father died when Friedrich was four, and he grew up in a household of devout women: his mother, grandmother, aunts and his sister Elisabeth, who will play a dark role in tomorrow's lesson. He was a brilliant pupil at the elite boarding school of Schulpforta and went on to study classical philology, the scholarly study of ancient Greek and Latin texts.

He was so gifted that in 1869, aged only twenty-four and before he had formally completed his doctorate, he was appointed professor of classical philology at the University of Basel in Switzerland. As a student in Leipzig he had stumbled on Schopenhauer's *The World as Will and Representation* in a second-hand bookshop and was electrified (remember Schopenhauer's blind, striving Will on Day 60). In Switzerland he became close to the composer Richard Wagner, another Schopenhauer enthusiast. His first book, *The Birth of Tragedy* (1872), argued that Greek tragedy arose from a tension between the Apollonian (order, form, dream) and the Dionysian (frenzy, intoxication, the dissolution of the self), and that Socrates' faith in reason had helped kill it. Fellow scholars were scandalized.

Nietzsche suffered for most of his adult life from crippling headaches, eye problems and stomach trouble. In 1879 he resigned his professorship on a small pension and spent the next decade wandering between boarding houses in Switzerland, Italy and the south of France, writing book after book that almost nobody bought: *The Gay Science* (1882), *Thus Spoke Zarathustra* (1883–85), *Beyond Good and Evil* (1886), *On the Genealogy of Morality* (1887) and, in a frantic final year, *Twilight of the Idols*, whose subtitle is "How to Philosophize with a Hammer."

In January 1889, in Turin, he suffered a complete mental collapse. (A famous story says it began when he threw his arms around a horse being whipped in the street; it is often repeated but rests on later, unreliable reports, so treat it as legend.) He never recovered and died in Weimar in 1900, cared for by his mother and then his sister, just as his fame was beginning.

sections.heading: God Is Dead: What It Means and Why It Matters
sections.body:
"God is dead" is not a metaphysical claim that a being once existed and then died. It is a cultural diagnosis. Nietzsche means that belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable for educated Europeans. Science, historical criticism of the Bible (which Nietzsche the philologist knew well), Darwin and the general spirit of the age had eroded it. People still went to church and still used Christian moral language, but the living faith that once organized the whole of life was gone.

Why, then, does the madman speak of murder? Because, Nietzsche thinks, Christianity's own virtues did the killing. Christianity taught truthfulness, and that very intellectual honesty eventually turned on Christianity itself and found it could not believe. We killed God with the tools God gave us.

The crucial point is what follows. In the same passage, the madman asks what we were doing when we unchained the earth from its sun: is there still an up or down? Are we not straying through an infinite nothing? For a thousand years European values, ideas of good and evil, meaning, purpose and the worth of each human soul, had been anchored in God. Remove the anchor, and those values are left floating. Many of Nietzsche's contemporaries, especially in England, thought they could drop God but keep Christian morality intact; he mocked George Eliot for exactly this. For Nietzsche that is like sawing off the branch you sit on and expecting to stay in the air.

The danger he foresaw was **nihilism**: the condition in which the highest values devalue themselves and people come to feel that nothing really matters. He predicted that this crisis would unfold over the next two centuries. He did not welcome nihilism; he wanted to diagnose it and, eventually, overcome it. But overcoming it required first understanding where our values came from. That is the job of genealogy.

sections.heading: Genealogy: Asking Where Values Come From
sections.body:
A **genealogy** is a family tree. Nietzsche's *On the Genealogy of Morality* (1887) traces the family tree of our moral ideas, asking under what historical and psychological conditions human beings invented the values "good" and "evil," and what those values have done for, and to, the people who hold them.

This is a different question from the one asked by most moral philosophers we have met. Kant (Day 56) asked what reason demands of every rational being. Bentham and Mill (Day 61) asked what produces the greatest happiness. Both took for granted that our ordinary moral convictions, kindness, humility, equality, compassion, were basically on the right track and simply needed a solid foundation. Nietzsche asks a more suspicious question: what if those convictions have a disreputable origin? What if they were born not from love or reason but from weakness, envy and the desire for revenge?

You might object that this commits the **genetic fallacy**, the mistake of judging an idea by its origin rather than its merits. A theory discovered in a dream can still be true. Nietzsche's defenders reply that moral values are not like scientific theories. Their authority over us depends partly on the story we tell about them, that they come from God, or from pure reason. If genealogy shows a different, all-too-human origin, it can loosen their grip and let us ask the question Nietzsche really cared about: what is the *value* of our values? Do they make human life stronger, richer and more creative, or weaker and sicker?

The *Genealogy* has three essays. The first, on "good and evil" versus "good and bad," is the most famous and the focus of our next section. The second traces the bad conscience and guilt back to debt; Nietzsche notes that the German word *Schuld* means both guilt and debt. The third examines the "ascetic ideal," the strange prestige of self-denial among priests, philosophers and even scientists, and ends with the haunting line that humanity would rather will nothingness than not will at all.

sections.heading: Master Morality and Slave Morality
sections.body:
Nietzsche asks us to imagine two original types of valuation.

**Master morality** belonged to ancient aristocrats: warriors and rulers such as the heroes of Homer. They began with themselves. They looked at their own strength, health, pride, generosity and boldness and called it "good," meaning roughly noble, excellent, fortunate. "Bad" was an afterthought: a mildly contemptuous word for what was common, weak or wretched, more like "lowly" than "wicked." Nietzsche points out that in Greek and other languages, words for good often originally meant noble or well-born.

**Slave morality**, by contrast, belonged to those who were powerless and oppressed. Nietzsche's prime example is ancient Judaism and the Christianity that grew from it, which he describes, provocatively, as a priestly people under foreign domination. Unable to defeat their masters in reality, they took an "imaginary revenge" by revaluing values. They began not with themselves but with the hated other: the strong, proud oppressor is **evil**. Then, as a reaction, they called themselves good: the meek, the humble, the patient, the suffering. The meek shall inherit the earth; the last shall be first.

Nietzsche calls this the "slave revolt in morality," and he thinks it won. Today we instinctively feel that humility, pity and equality are moral and that pride is a sin. That feeling is, he suggests, the victory of the slave revaluation.

His parable makes the logic vivid. Lambs dislike birds of prey; that is understandable. But when the lambs say "birds of prey are evil, so whatever is least like a bird of prey, a lamb, must be good," they make a sly move. They imagine that the eagle *chose* to be strong and could have chosen to be meek, so that weakness becomes a moral achievement rather than a condition.

Two cautions. First, Nietzsche does not simply celebrate the masters; he calls them in some ways stupid and shallow, and admits that the priestly slave revolt made humanity "deep" and interesting for the first time. Second, his descriptions of Jews, priests and ancient peoples are sweeping and polemical, not careful history, and they have been read in ugly ways, a story we take up tomorrow.

sections.heading: Ressentiment: The Morality of Revenge
sections.body:
The engine of slave morality is a psychological state Nietzsche calls **ressentiment**. He uses the French word on purpose, because it suggests something deeper and more poisonous than ordinary resentment.

Ressentiment is the festering hostility of people who feel injured and powerless and cannot act out their anger. Unable to strike back, they turn the anger inward and into imagination. It becomes a slow, brooding preoccupation with the enemy, a desire for revenge disguised as a desire for justice. Nietzsche says the slave revolt in morality begins when ressentiment itself becomes creative and gives birth to values.

The noble type, by contrast, forgets quickly. Nietzsche imagines such a person shrugging off insults that would make a weaker person brood for years. That is not because the noble person is a saint, but because he is busy living and acting rather than reacting.

What makes ressentiment so interesting as a psychological concept is its disguise. It does not say "I am weak and envious." It says "I am good, and they are evil." It can present spite as righteousness and passivity as virtue. Nietzsche thinks we should be suspicious whenever moral indignation is suspiciously enjoyable, whenever a person seems to need an enemy in order to feel good about themselves.

This connects to the second essay's story about guilt. Over centuries, Nietzsche argues, civilization forced aggressive human instincts that could no longer be discharged outward to turn back against the self. The result was the **bad conscience**, which priests then interpreted as sin and guilt before God, a debt that could never be repaid. Here Nietzsche anticipates Freud's later idea of a punishing super-ego, and his technique of reading hidden motives beneath respectable surfaces is why the philosopher Paul Ricoeur grouped him with Marx (Day 63) and Freud as one of the three "masters of suspicion." Marx unmasked ideology as serving class interest; Nietzsche unmasked morality as serving the will of the weak.

sections.heading: Perspectivism, and the Objections
sections.body:
If values have histories, what about truth itself? Nietzsche's view is usually called **perspectivism**. In the third essay of the *Genealogy* he writes that there is only a perspectival seeing, only a perspectival "knowing"; the more eyes, different eyes, we can bring to bear on a matter, the more complete our concept of it will be. In an unpublished notebook he went further: against those who say "there are only facts," he replied that there are no facts, only interpretations.

This is easily misunderstood as "anything goes." But the passage in the *Genealogy* actually says that *more* perspectives give a *better* understanding, which only makes sense if some interpretations are better than others. Many scholars read Nietzsche as denying a "view from nowhere," a God's-eye standpoint free of all interests, while still allowing that we can know more or less, and see more or less honestly. Every knower is a living creature with needs, drives and a point of view; knowledge is always somebody's knowledge, for some purpose. Compare Kant (Day 55), who said we know the world only as structured by our minds; Nietzsche makes the structuring messier, more biological and more plural.

Now the objections:

- **Self-refutation.** If there are no facts, only interpretations, is *that* a fact? Nietzsche anticipated the jab and replied, in effect, "so much the better" (*Beyond Good and Evil* 22 even concedes his own view is "only interpretation"). Critics find this evasive.
- **The genetic fallacy.** Even if compassion arose partly from ressentiment, that does not show compassion is bad today. Mill could reply that kindness produces happiness regardless of its family tree.
- **Bad history.** As history, the slave revolt story is a sweeping myth, and its treatment of Judaism in particular is a caricature. Defenders respond that it is a psychological parable, not a work of scholarship.
- **Who decides what is healthy?** Nietzsche judges values by whether they promote strong, flourishing life. But that standard is itself a value; why should it escape genealogy?

Whatever you conclude, Nietzsche changed the questions. After him, philosophers could not easily assume that morality floats free of history, psychology and power. Michel Foucault (Day 81) would call his own historical studies "genealogies" in Nietzsche's honor. Tomorrow we turn from Nietzsche the destroyer to Nietzsche the would-be creator: will to power, the Übermensch and eternal recurrence.

keyQuote.text: God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him.
keyQuote.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science (1882), section 125 (trans. Walter Kaufmann)

modernConnection.title: Ressentiment and the Outrage Economy
modernConnection.body:
Many commentators across the political spectrum have reached for Nietzsche's concept of ressentiment to describe online life. Social media platforms tend to reward posts that provoke anger and moral indignation, because outrage spreads. Researchers such as William Brady and colleagues have found that moral-emotional words tend to increase how widely posts are shared. The result is a public sphere in which people can spend hours rehearsing grievances against enemies they will never meet.

Nietzsche would ask uncomfortable questions here. When we pile on someone who has said something offensive, how much is concern for justice and how much is the pleasure of feeling righteous? Do some online identities, on the left and the right, define themselves chiefly by what they hate, so that the enemy is needed to give the group its sense of being good? That is precisely the structure he described: "they are evil, therefore we are good." Political analysts have used ressentiment to explain the appeal of populist movements that mobilize feelings of humiliation and being looked down on by elites, and also to criticize movements that, as critics see it, turn victimhood into a source of moral status.

Nietzsche also helps diagnose a quieter phenomenon: people who have lost religious belief but still feel the full weight of moral judgment, guilt and the hunger for redemption, now attached to diet, productivity or political purity. The madman's question, whether we can keep the values after losing their foundation, is still open.

But be careful. Ressentiment is a dangerously convenient weapon: it lets you dismiss any complaint about injustice as mere envy of the strong. Real oppression produces real grievances, and a just demand for fair treatment is not ressentiment just because the person making it is angry. Nietzsche himself had little sympathy for democratic and egalitarian movements, so using his concept responsibly means applying it to yourself first, and remembering that the question "is this claim true?" does not disappear because we have identified the emotion behind it.

vocabulary.definition: Nietzsche's diagnosis that belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable in modern Europe, leaving the values built on that belief without a foundation.
vocabulary.example: For Nietzsche, the death of God was not good news to be celebrated but an earthquake whose aftershocks would last for centuries.

vocabulary.definition: The condition in which the highest values lose their authority and life seems to have no meaning, purpose or worth.
vocabulary.example: Nietzsche feared that once people stopped believing in God, nihilism would spread through European culture.

vocabulary.definition: Nietzsche's method of tracing the historical and psychological origins of values in order to question their authority and assess their worth.
vocabulary.example: A genealogy of politeness might ask what social pressures first made people value good manners.

vocabulary.definition: A noble system of valuation that begins by affirming oneself as 'good' (excellent, strong) and regards the lowly as merely 'bad.'
vocabulary.example: Homer's heroes, proud of their strength and glory, embody what Nietzsche called master morality.

vocabulary.definition: A system of valuation born from the powerless that begins by condemning the strong as 'evil' and then calls the meek and humble 'good.'
vocabulary.example: Nietzsche argued that praising humility and pity while condemning pride is the signature of slave morality.

vocabulary.definition: A festering, powerless hostility toward those seen as superior, which turns into imaginary revenge and can disguise itself as moral righteousness.
vocabulary.example: He claimed to care only about fairness, but his obsession with his successful rival looked more like ressentiment.

vocabulary.definition: Nietzsche's view that all knowing is from a particular perspective shaped by needs and interests, with no neutral 'view from nowhere.'
vocabulary.example: According to perspectivism, a doctor, a painter and a farmer each see a different but genuine aspect of the same landscape.

vocabulary.definition: The error of judging an idea true or false, good or bad, merely because of where it came from.
vocabulary.example: Rejecting a medicine because it was first discovered by accident would be a genetic fallacy.

thinkingExercise.title: A Genealogy of One of Your Values
thinkingExercise.prompt: Choose a moral value you hold strongly, such as honesty, humility, fairness, compassion or hard work. Spend 10 to 15 minutes writing its 'family tree' in Nietzsche's suspicious style, and then test whether the value survives.
steps: Write down the value and one sentence on why you believe it is good.
Trace its origin in your own life: who taught it to you, in what situations, and what did holding it do for you or for them? Did it ever serve someone's power or comfort?
Now play Nietzsche: write the least flattering possible story about how this value might have arisen in human history, for example from fear, envy or a desire to control others.
Play the critic of Nietzsche: does that unflattering story actually show the value is bad today, or would that be a genetic fallacy? Write a reply.
Conclude: has your confidence in the value changed? Do you now hold it differently, for example more consciously or for different reasons?

summary: Nietzsche (1844–1900), a classical philologist turned philosopher, wrote most of his works in a decade of illness and wandering before collapsing in 1889.
'God is dead' is a cultural diagnosis: belief has become impossible for modern Europeans, yet they have not grasped that values built on God are now unanchored, threatening nihilism.
Genealogy traces the origins of values to ask about their worth, not just their justification.
Master morality affirms the strong as 'good' and the lowly as 'bad'; slave morality, driven by ressentiment, condemns the strong as 'evil' and calls the meek 'good.'
Perspectivism denies a view from nowhere but, on careful readings, still allows some perspectives to be richer than others.
Major objections include the genetic fallacy, historical caricature, self-refutation and the question of what grounds Nietzsche's own standard of 'healthy' life.

quiz.question: In The Gay Science, who does the madman address when he announces that God is dead?
options: Priests in a cathedral
Philosophy students at a university
A crowd of unbelievers in a marketplace who laugh at him
The emperor and his court
quiz.explanation: He speaks to people who already do not believe in God; Nietzsche's point is that even unbelievers have not grasped the consequences of God's death.

quiz.question: What did Nietzsche mean by saying 'God is dead'?
options: Belief in the Christian God had become impossible for modern European culture, with enormous consequences for its values
A supreme being literally existed and then ceased to exist
Science had proved mathematically that God does not exist
Churches had been banned by the German state
quiz.explanation: It is a cultural diagnosis rather than a metaphysical event: faith had lost its power, leaving morality without its traditional foundation.

quiz.question: Nietzsche thought people could easily abandon belief in God while keeping Christian morality exactly as it was.
quiz.explanation: He mocked this idea (for example in George Eliot); he thought Christian values depended on Christian belief and would be shaken by its loss.

quiz.question: According to Nietzsche, how does slave morality create its values?
options: By first affirming its own strength and then calling the weak 'bad'
By calculating the greatest happiness of the greatest number
By deriving duties from pure reason alone
By first condemning the powerful as 'evil' and then defining itself as 'good' in reaction
quiz.explanation: Slave morality starts from a 'No' to the hated other; master morality starts from a 'Yes' to oneself.

quiz.question: A coworker who never confronts the boss spends years privately brooding over him, calls him a moral monster, and describes her own passivity as a mark of superior virtue. Which Nietzschean concept best fits?
options: Amor fati
Ressentiment
Master morality
Apollonian order
quiz.explanation: Ressentiment is powerless hostility that cannot act and instead takes imaginary revenge, recasting weakness as virtue.

quiz.question: Which objection claims that Nietzsche's genealogy cannot, by itself, show that compassion is bad?
options: The genetic fallacy: an idea's origin does not settle its value
The is-ought gap
The problem of induction
The Third Man argument
quiz.explanation: Critics argue that even if compassion arose from weakness or envy, its worth today is a separate question. Defenders reply that moral authority depends partly on origin stories.

quiz.question: Nietzsche noted that the German word Schuld means both 'guilt' and 'debt,' and used this to trace the origin of the bad conscience.
quiz.explanation: The second essay of the Genealogy connects moral guilt to older relations of creditor and debtor.

quiz.question: Which statement best captures a careful reading of Nietzsche's perspectivism?
options: Every opinion is exactly as good as every other
Only scientific measurements are real knowledge
There is no view from nowhere, but bringing more perspectives to bear can give a fuller understanding
Reality does not exist at all
quiz.explanation: In the Genealogy (III.12) he says more eyes give a more complete concept, which implies some interpretations are better, not that anything goes.

quiz.question: Paul Ricoeur grouped Nietzsche with which two thinkers as 'masters of suspicion'?
options: Kant and Hegel
Plato and Aristotle
Kierkegaard and Schopenhauer
Marx and Freud
quiz.explanation: All three looked beneath respectable surfaces for hidden motives: class interest for Marx, unconscious drives for Freud, the will of the weak for Nietzsche.

quiz.question: The story that Nietzsche's collapse in Turin began when he embraced a horse being whipped is well documented by reliable eyewitness evidence.
quiz.explanation: The horse story is famous but rests on later, unreliable reports, so it is best treated as legend.

goDeeper.body:
Scholars disagree sharply about what kind of philosopher Nietzsche was. One tradition, shaped by Walter Kaufmann after the Second World War, presented him as an existentialist humanist calling individuals to self-creation. Another, associated with Heidegger, read him as the last metaphysician, whose 'will to power' completed rather than escaped the Western tradition. French thinkers such as Gilles Deleuze and Michel Foucault read him as a philosopher of difference and power. More recently, Anglo-American scholars like Brian Leiter have defended a 'naturalist' Nietzsche, a moral psychologist who explains human values in terms of drives, types and causes much as a scientist would, while Bernard Williams's *Truth and Truthfulness* took up genealogy as a tool that can vindicate some values, such as truthfulness, rather than only debunk them.

Another debate concerns whether Nietzsche is a moral 'error theorist' who thinks all moral claims are false, or a revaluer who wants new and better values. The answer affects how we read perspectivism, too: is it a radical theory of truth or a modest point about the interests behind inquiry? Maudemarie Clark's influential work argues that Nietzsche's later writings move away from denying truth altogether.

Finally, consider the relationship between genealogy and justification. Kant would insist that whether a maxim can be universalized has nothing to do with how anyone came to believe it. Nietzsche thinks that pretending values have no history is itself a symptom of what he calls the philosophers' lack of historical sense. Who has the better of this exchange may depend on whether you think morality is more like mathematics or more like a language.

Is it possible to keep values like human equality and compassion without the religious framework in which they first developed?
